In [[group theory]], a '''word''' is any written product of [[group (mathematics)|group]] elements and their inverses.  For example, if ''x'', ''y'' and ''z'' are elements of a group ''G'', then ''xy'', ''z''<sup>−1</sup>''xzz'' and ''y''<sup>−1</sup>''zxx''<sup>−1</sup>''yz''<sup>−1</sup> are words in the set {''x'',&nbsp;''y'',&nbsp;''z''}.  Two different words may evaluate to the same value in ''G'',<ref>for example, f<sub>d</sub>r<sub>1</sub> and r<sub>1</sub>f<sub>c</sub> in the [[Group (mathematics)#Second example: a symmetry group|group of square symmetries]]</ref> or even in every group.<ref>for example, ''xy'' and ''xzz''<sup>−1</sup>''y''</ref>  Words play an important role in the theory of [[free group]]s and [[presentation of a group|presentations]], and are central objects of study in [[combinatorial group theory]].

==Definitions==
Let ''G'' be a group, and let ''S'' be a [[subset]] of ''G''.  A '''word in ''S''''' is any [[Term (logic)|expression]] of the form
:<math>s_1^{\varepsilon_1} s_2^{\varepsilon_2} \cdots s_n^{\varepsilon_n}</math>
where ''s''<sub>1</sub>,...,''s<sub>n</sub>'' are elements of ''S'', called '''generators''', and each ''ε<sub>i</sub>'' is ±1.  The number ''n'' is known as the '''length''' of the word.

Each word in ''S'' represents an element of ''G'', namely the product of the expression.  By convention, the unique<ref>[[Group (mathematics)#Uniqueness of identity element and inverses|Uniqueness of identity element and inverses]]</ref> [[identity element]] can be represented by the '''empty word''', which is the unique word of length zero.

==Notation==
When writing words, it is common to use [[exponentiation|exponential]] notation as an abbreviation.  For example, the word
:<math>x x y^{-1} z y z z z x^{-1} x^{-1} \,</math>
could be written as
:<math>x^2 y^{-1} z y z^3 x^{-2}. \,</math>
This latter expression is not a word itself&mdash;it is simply a shorter notation for the original.

When dealing with long words, it can be helpful to use an [[overline]] to denote inverses of elements of ''S''.  Using overline notation, the above word would be written as follows:
:<math>x^2\overline{y}zyz^3\overline{x}^2. \,</math>

==Reduced words==
Any word in which a generator appears next to its own inverse (''xx''<sup>−1</sup> or ''x''<sup>−1</sup>''x'') can be simplified by omitting the redundant pair:
:<math>y^{-1}zxx^{-1}y\;\;\longrightarrow\;\;y^{-1}zy.</math>
This operation is known as '''reduction''', and it does not change the group element represented by the word.  Reductions can be thought of as relations (defined [[#Relations|below]]) that follow from the [[Group_(mathematics)#Definition|group axioms]].

A '''reduced word''' is a word that contains no redundant pairs.  Any word can be simplified to a reduced word by performing a sequence of reductions:
:<math>xzy^{-1}xx^{-1}yz^{-1}zz^{-1}yz\;\;\longrightarrow\;\;xyz.</math>
The result does not depend on the order in which the reductions are performed.

A word is '''cyclically reduced''' [[if and only if]] every [[cyclic permutation]] of the word is reduced.

==Operations on words==
The '''product''' of two words is obtained by concatenation:
:<math>\left(xzyz^{-1}\right)\left(zy^{-1}x^{-1}y\right) = xzyz^{-1}zy^{-1}x^{-1}y.</math>
Even if the two words are reduced, the product may not be.

The '''inverse''' of a word is obtained by inverting each generator, and reversing the order of the elements:
:<math>\left(zy^{-1}x^{-1}y\right)^{-1}=y^{-1}xyz^{-1}.</math>
The product of a word with its inverse can be reduced to the empty word:
:<math>zy^{-1}x^{-1}y \; y^{-1}xyz^{-1} = 1.</math>

You can move a generator from the beginning to the end of a word by [[conjugation (group theory)|conjugation]]:
:<math>x^{-1}\left(xy^{-1}z^{-1}yz\right)x = y^{-1}z^{-1}yzx.</math>

==Generating set of a group==
{{main|Generating set of a group}}
A subset ''S'' of a group ''G'' is called a '''generating set''' if every element of ''G'' can be represented by a word in ''S''.

When ''S'' is not a generating set for ''G'', the set of elements represented by words in ''S'' is a [[subgroup]] of ''G'', known as the '''subgroup of ''G'' generated by ''S''''' and usually denoted <math>\langle S\rangle</math>.  It is the smallest subgroup of ''G'' that contains the elements of ''S''.

==Normal forms==
A '''[[normal form (mathematics)|normal form]]''' for a group ''G'' with generating set ''S'' is a choice of one reduced word in ''S'' for each element of ''G''.  For example:
* The words 1, ''i'', ''j'', ''ij'' are a normal form for the [[Klein four-group]] with {{math|1=''S'' = {''i'', &nbsp;''j''}}} &nbsp;and 1 representing the empty word (the identity element for the group).
* The words 1, ''r'', ''r''<sup>2</sup>, ..., ''r<sup>n-1</sup>'', ''s'', ''sr'', ..., ''sr<sup>n-1</sup>'' are a normal form for the [[dihedral group]] Dih<sub>''n''</sub> with {{math|1=''S'' = {''s'', &nbsp;''r''}}} &nbsp;and 1 as above.
* The set of words of the form ''x<sup>m</sup>y<sup>n</sup>'' for ''m,n''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''Z''' are a normal form for the [[direct product of groups|direct product]] of the [[cyclic group]]s {{angbr|''x''}} and {{angbr|''y''}} with {{math|1=''S'' = {''x'', &nbsp;''y''}}}.
* The set of reduced words in ''S'' are the unique [[Normal form for free groups and free product of groups|normal form for the free group]] over ''S''.
{{anchor|Relations}}
==Relations and presentations==
{{main|Presentation of a group}}
If ''S'' is a generating set for a group ''G'', a '''relation''' is a pair of words in ''S'' that represent the same element of ''G''.  These are usually written as equations, e.g. <math>x^{-1} y x = y^2.\,</math>
A set <math>\mathcal{R}</math> of relations '''defines ''G''''' if every relation in ''G'' follows logically from those in <math>\mathcal{R}</math> using the [[group (mathematics)#Definition|axioms for a group]].  A '''presentation''' for ''G'' is a pair <math>\langle S \mid \mathcal{R}\rangle</math>, where ''S'' is a generating set for ''G'' and <math>\mathcal{R}</math> is a defining set of relations.

For example, the [[Klein four-group]] can be defined by the presentation
:<math>\langle i,j \mid i^2 = 1,\,j^2 = 1,\,ij=ji\rangle.</math>
Here 1 denotes the empty word, which represents the identity element.

==Free groups==
{{main|Free group}}
If ''S'' is any set, the '''free group over ''S''''' is the group with presentation <math>\langle S\mid\;\rangle</math>.  That is, the free group over ''S'' is the group generated by the elements of ''S'', with no extra relations.  Every element of the free group can be written uniquely as a reduced word in ''S''.
